utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning, everybody. The case may be called, please. And in the meantime, the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, please. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, Mr. John Ostojic, and Mr. Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Kapetanovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We proceed with the cross-examination of Mr. Kapetanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kapetanovic. My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. John Ostojic, I am representing the Defence of Dr. Stakic before this Tribunal. The Defence of Mr. Stakic would first like to clear up certain issues concerning your previous statements, and I should like to have the assistance of the usher, please, for the witness to be given the statements that he had previously given to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Chamber has drawn to my attention that you have some difficulty in reading, Mr. Kapetanovic, and we will try to avoid having to read the statements. But let me just ask you to take the English version of your statement which is in front of you, and to tell us whether you can recognise your signature on these statements, if you can. If not, we will move on.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The signatures are all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do recognise your signatures. You gave two statements to the officials of the Tribunal. I apologise. The interpreters have not heard your response.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, once again, we haven't heard the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness hasn't answered because there hasn't been a question put to him. There was simply a statement that there were statements to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was waiting for further explanation. I didn't see a question there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give two statements to the officials of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give them on your own free will?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone force you to say anything?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any pressure whatsoever exerted by the officials of the Tribunal on you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This has been already answered.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us with the following, please: When did you sign the second statement -- strike that. When did you sign the first statement with respect to the time you gave your second statement?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's very important in this case. If you have any specific questions, please ask them. With the permission of the Court, let me -- I should also like to add something that I failed to mention yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, would you be so kind, please, and answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, let us stay in correct order. You asked an extremely difficult question taking into account there are dates on the two documents, but the witness asked for some space to give some explanation as regards the statement yesterday, and of course he has the right to do this immediately. Please, Mr. Kapetanovic, proceed, if you have anything to add to your statement yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the gentleman from the Defence should listen to what I have to say. Despite some provocation, I need to ask the Court that Honourable Judges do not take into account any statement which would cause Mr. Stakic to spend longer time in prison just because of Nijaz Kapetanovic, and just as God is merciful, I should like to appeal to the Court to have understanding for what I have been through, and that despite that, I have this right. I know that some Bosniaks would not be very happy with my attitude here. I do not have the right to exonerate him on behalf of other people. We have all been through a number of trials in our lives. I am a man always willing to pardon and to show understanding of the problems of others. That is what I had to say, and I should like to ask the Defence to ask specific questions if they have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would the Defence please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I tried to be clear, but I was not probably as clear as was necessary. I just wanted to ask you whether the first statement was initially shown to you before you gave your second statement, and did the first statement help you when giving the second statement?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's very important. Yes, I was shown this statement, but I don't remember saying anything that would be mutually exclusive, anything that would be contrary to what I had previously said. I may have repeated certain things, but as far as I know, there are no many discrepancies in my statements. I don't know whether you've had the opportunity to read the statement, the English version of the statement, that is. I myself didn't read the statement. It was from the interpreter that I learned about the contents of the English version of the statement. It may have been a good idea for me to see it in my language, but I don't think that after the second statement that there should be any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I try to give you the B/C/S copy, that is how we refer to your language. However, because it appears that you have some difficulty with reading, I'm not going to trouble you with the reading of this statement. I will just show you some portions of the statements. The only reason why I showed you the English version of the statement was because that is the only version that actually bears your signature, not the B/C/S version. In the statement that you gave in December 1997, you stated that you were a politician by occupation. That is what we can read in the statement. Was that a correct statement at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was active in the party, and I considered politics to be my occupation at the time. Later on, I was back in the field of education. But as I was active in the party, I was on the party's payroll, and I considered myself a professional politician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement given in December 1997, three last digits, 739, paragraph 3, pages -- lines 14, 15, 18, and 19, of the B/C/S version page 3, the last paragraph, lines 6, 7, and 10 of the English version of the text, you speak about Dr. Kovacevic, and you say the following, I quote: "I saw him once on the news of the Belgrade TV, which was probably in January or February 1992. When the war broke out in Croatia, I saw that he was a guest in the programmes which were broadcast by the Belgrade television." When did you give -- when did you see Dr. Kovacevic? Can you be more specific, on the Belgrade TV?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was either in January or February 1992. That was my opinion at the time, and I still maintain that opinion. I don't see a problem there because one could watch the Belgrade TV in Prijedor at the time because it was transmitted over the local television transmitter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen him before that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I had. I had seen him in hospital, for example, and I had also seen him attending some meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But had you seen him on TV prior to that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When some news were broadcast from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which TV was it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think it could have been Utel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was transmitted over the Sarajevo TV. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, via transmitters which were located throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were programmes from battlefields, broadcast in Sarajevo and elsewhere. Nusret Sivac, a local journalist, was, for example, one of them, who was the reporter in these programmes. And he was allowed to report the news concerning Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that you had been a student at several different universities?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. In Rijeka, Tuzla, Sarajevo, Banja Luka, and I was also a guest professor. I taught computer science. Actually, attended courses in computer science for one month. It was a specialist training. We changed universities, and that is how I spent one month in Banja Luka and one month in Sarajevo. It was organised by the institute of education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. It may seem that I am not pleased with the answer, but what I'm actually doing is waiting for the interpretation to finish and text which appears on the screen to stop so that we can move on and so that others can follow us. You testified yesterday that you wanted to help with the founding of the SDA and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was my desire to help found as many political parties as possible. The Serbs had already established the SDS, and the SDA had been set up, and I want the HDZ, that is, the Croats, to have their political party founded in the area as well. I was aware of the situation. I was aware of how people felt, that they felt threatened, both Croats and Serbs, and Bosniaks, of course, because of the prevailing circumstances and the overall situation. But Croats were afraid of founding the HDZ, and they wanted to become members of the SDA which, in my opinion, was not a very good thing because they would have eventually felt compelled to join the SDA. There were several thousands of them in Prijedor, and they were a minority. So they had reasons to feel threatened, and that is why I wanted to encourage them to establish their own political party. Serbs were also very active politically at the time, and I attended many of their rallies. I don't know exactly what you're interested in concerning this particular issue. Like I said, it was my desire to have as many multiethnic and multicultural organisations in town as possible, and I didn't want the pressure of the communist party to continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The national parties, did they form a coalition to oppose the communist party?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were coalitions in the municipality of Prijedor. There were agreements between the SDS and the SDA, for example, agreements which were eventually signed. You said that the parties were national parties or nationalistic parties. I wouldn't exactly call them nationalistic parties. It is true that in certain of their aspects they could have been perhaps described as nationalistic, but I think that it can also be considered to be a positive development because any such feelings were suppressed during the communist regime. Whether everyone was pleased with the coalition and with these agreements, I don't know because I attended only two or three such meetings, in particular at the time when Srdjo Srdic was the president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This informal coalition, did it exist prior to the elections? Did you know that an attempt would be made to topple the communist regime jointly?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't want, for instance, any SDA poster to be put on top of an SDS poster and cover it. So both formally and informally, there was an agreement between these two parties, and I was very pleased with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SDS and SDA politicians, did they support each other in their preelectoral meetings and rallies?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. I mean, I did not attend all of the rallies. It was impossible for me to be everywhere, but generally speaking yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement given in December 1997, on page 3, last paragraph, line 2 of the English version of the text, page 739, paragraph 3, line 10 of the B/C/S version, when you speak about Kovacevic and his preelection speeches, you declare the following: "He said that it is now time for the Serbs to take revenge." Now, how does this fit into your explanations about the coalition and the mutual support?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we didn't hear witness's answer. Could the witness please be asked to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. The interpreters couldn't hear your answer from the beginning. Could you please restart with your answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay in the booth? Thank you. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that there was a misunderstanding in this interview. Mr. Kovacevic, prior to the elections, rarely said such things. I think that this is something that he said after the elections, at the time when public offices were being divided up. At the time when the situation had already become problematic. I don't know if there's anything else I can help you with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was not entered into the record here, but it seems to me that you said that the word "revenge" was never mentioned in the -- during the preelectoral campaign.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the written statement contains the information that Kovacevic made such a statement during the preelectoral campaign, you would say that this was then not correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement of December 1997, page 4, paragraph 2, lines 2, 3, 4 of the English version; 739, second-last paragraph, line 2 of the B/C/S version, you say, and I quote: "Serbs, in their villages, marked certain spots near their houses with a triangle, and those were probably places where weapons should be unloaded." Can you please tell us where did Serbs do that, in which village?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said yesterday. These were the places with mixed population with the either prevailing -- Muslims as the prevailing population or Serbs as the prevailing population, and we did ourselves go and see and we did see such markings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the person next to whose house such marking was made?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you any names at this stage, because I was not so much interested at the time. But I did see these markings next to some 20 houses. It was very difficult for me to remember the names because I really wanted to just move on from that particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What characterised these triangles?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were around a metre to 1.5 metres in dimension, and they pointed to the house where -- which obviously was to be left intact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they made of? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were made of wooden -- small wooden planks such as used for the fence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the -- how were the weapons brought to that place, do you know?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not really pay much attention, but I think it was done with the JNA vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, page 43, line 23 of the transcript of your yesterday's statement, this is where you said that wooden crosses were placed in order for the helicopters to fly over them.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were pointing the direction to which the helicopters were to land to deliver weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So both the triangles and crosses were placed?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the crosses placed?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see. When we were going through Trnopolje, through Kozarusa, this is where we were able to see such markings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you personally did not see them?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not personally see them. Some of my colleagues who -- saw that, and all the places where it was possible for a helicopter to land, these were the places that were usually marked. I said yesterday that the Bosniaks were also arming themselves because they needed the arms. So obviously, some of the people from the JNA were selling weapons also to the Bosniaks. No wonder, then, that they were giving weapons to Serbs as well. However, I did not say that Mr. Stakic knew or knows about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please go back now to the time of the negotiations about the division of power. You say that you participated in three such meetings.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said two or three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if minutes were made of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not throughout the time of the meetings; only when something was agreed on. This was the point when it was noted down, but the discussion itself was not taken down in minutes. So when the discussion was going on, persons were taking down notes on their own initiative, and then it was only when something was agreed on that it was noted down officially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who signed the minutes that were taken down by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we didn't hear the second part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the second part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There's an objection to the question, because it assumes a fact that there's no evidence that the SDA took the minutes. The witness simply said that when something was agreed, it was written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I might be of assistance, Your Honours. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but here I have to give a comment on behalf of all the Judges. It's a question of principle raised by the OTP. And of course, we are prepared, and we will proceed this way: No longer to allow what has been custom in this courtroom until now to have the answer already included in the question. Such kinds of suggestive questions will never be allowed for both parties in future. And therefore, the objection of the OTP is sustained. Please proceed, Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to explain that my question was misinterpreted. I did not ask whether the SDA kept the minutes, but who was it that signed the minutes on behalf the SDA. I think the witness can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the last question. My answer was Mirza Mujadzic. I cannot recall anyone else signing it but him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you remember, which body elected Mr. Muhamed Cehajic to the function of the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the deputies of the assembly, the Municipal Assembly itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which body elected or appointed Mr. Hasan Talundzic to the position of the chief of the public security station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the result of the interparty agreement, and it was confirmed by the Municipal Assembly. I told you that later on, I was no longer involved in the political life as I became the president of Merhamet. I won't be able to give you the exact details, but I can tell you what I think the case was, and I will emphasise in my response whether I think or I am sure that this is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4, paragraph 6 of the English version; that is page 740, paragraph 3 of the B/C/S version, you speak of the 30th April and the takeover of power by the SDS. And you say that "Serbs were shooting in the air in the morning." Was this really the case? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was taken, yes. I don't know what the reason for that was, if when we were being taken in front of the theatre, they were shooting out into the air. Yes, this is correct. I don't know what their motives were. They weren't shooting at me or at any other person. If they had been shooting at me, I wouldn't be here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we talking about the morning of the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking about the day when the checkpoints were placed throughout the town, when the Serbs took over the power, when the attack took place actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're not talking about the 30th of April; we're talking about the 30th of May here?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, when it says in your statement that the people were shooting in the air on the 30th of April, this is incorrect. This actually took place on the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the president of Merhamet, were you able to move around the town?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to move around the town after the 30th of April until the town was actual -- came actually under attack. I would go to the offices of the Red Cross in Prijedor to try and coordinate the lists of people who were in greater need for aid so that I would be able to use these lists for the distribution of aid. I would go, then, through the local communities themselves, trying to draw up lists for the people. So yes, I was able to move freely until Prijedor came under attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct me if I am wrong: You remained in Prijedor until 1995?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you move around Prijedor after the attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not officially under any house arrest; I was just advised for my safety to stay at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which house did you spend this year -- that particular year?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spent that particular year in two houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the dates?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we talk about the attack on Prijedor, from the attack on Prijedor until November 1992, I was in this family house. And as of November 1992 until the 23rd of February 1995, this was the period that I spent in the house of a Bosniak. I cannot recall the name now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for about six months following the attack, you remained in your house?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And then another six months approximately in this other house. I didn't move around. Afterwards, I went to Merhamet on business. And from time to time, I visited some local communes to see how the work was going on, until 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during these six months after the attack, your house did not sustain any damage at all?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a moment. Only the windows were broken on one side of the house. The glass panes of several windows which was the result of the detonation when the church was blown up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were moved to this other house, you say that your own house was destroyed with a bulldozer?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated that this was done pursuant to an order of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least that is what I was told by the soldiers. I also indicated that I did not have any written document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the war presidency existed after the month of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There existed some kind of authority, some kind of war presidency. After all, the war was still going on, and all such institutions on both Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sides were called and referred to as "war presidencies." But as a result of the pressure by the international community, this was changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You describe in your statement an event which took place when you were in Prijedor and when you were approached by the son of the late Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. He approached Ibro Beglerbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is he approached the group in which you were, the group of people in which you were?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was with you on that day?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you a moment ago that I was with Dr. Ibrahim Beglerbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember who was there with you also?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point is, Mr. Kapetanovic, that you were not present when this took place.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you know that? You may have been present, too. What do you know?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Persons who were present at this event did not mention you as one of the people who was there.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just as I am not mentioning everybody who was present now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, this is a suggestive question, and we can't see the sources for the facts you want to insinuate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is the appropriate time but I wanted to clarify my objection because it goes to the whole process of how we do examination and cross-examination. Again, I would object to that question but not because it is suggestive but because it amounts to testimony by counsel about what other people said. Regarding the other question, I think it's wrong to ask a witness, for example, who took the minutes for the SDA when the witness hasn't said any minutes were taken by the SDA so how can he answer it. But I know there's a difference between the civil and common-law systems, or adversarial and inquisitorial systems regarding cross-examination and suggestive questions. I would not object to the Defence asking a question that's suggestive on cross-examination or vice versa, because, in my experience -- that's allowed in my system, of course -- but also in my experience, it limits the cross-examination tremendously and we can get answers to questions much more quickly than if we simply ask an open-ended question on cross-examination. I'm not afraid that too many of my witnesses are going to follow suggestions by Mr. Lukic, and I don't think he's afraid that his witnesses are going to follow my suggestions. If they disagree, they disagree. But it allows us to get the point in cross-examination much quicker if we're allowed to ask suggestive or leading questions in cross-examination. I don't know at what point Your Honour wants to take that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to decide on the last question and only on questions immediately before us. And here, I can't identify the source of your question, and therefore I would ask you probably to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We are not allowed to compare the statements of the witnesses, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably you can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If other witnesses who were present when this took place said that you were not present at the event, would they be wrong?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible for them to say so, but I don't think that I said anything that would contradict myself. It is possible that someone was there, and that I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am referring to the event when this group of people was approached by the son of Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there. I saw it with my own eyes. Or else I saw these things in my dreams. I mean, how would it be possible for me to describe this if I had not been present? I was very surprised. I was actually frightened. I was afraid of a potential incident. And I must say that I was very happy with the reaction of Mr. Beglerbegovic. He was very correct and fair in his reaction. I also understand the son of Mr. Kovacevic. I know that he's still mourning his father, and now know that it was all very difficult for him. I don't see anything wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to compare your statements, the one that you gave in 1997 and the one that you gave in 2001. I should like to hear your explanation on potential differences in these statements if any, and if there are such differences I should like to know your final testimony on the issue. In your 1997 statement, December 1997, on page 3, paragraph 3, middle of the page, in the middle of the page, or page 739, paragraph 2 of the B/C/S version, you declare the following: "Kovacevic was always mentioning that Prijedor was a Serb town, so there was no need to give Muslims any positions of authority." Whereas, in your statement given in 2001, on page 2, paragraph 5, or page 662, paragraph 5 of the B/C/S version, you declare the following: "Also, Stakic was mentioning that Prijedor was a Serb town and Serb land and that there was no need to give Muslims any positions of authority." My question is, who was it who stated this?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them did. So did Mr. Srdjo Srdic. He also said that Prijedor was a Serb town. I mean, that was the story that went around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the first, the second, the third, then the fourth said that.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you have in mind? You cannot adapt your testimony to the accused on trial.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said, and I am happy to repeat, that it was a common conviction amongst the Serbs that according to the census which was taken in 1991, that there had been more Serbs in Prijedor and that the Serbs were betrayed by the census and the election as well. This was a common statement amongst almost all Serbs in Prijedor, not only the first, the second, the third, and the fourth one. I see no reason for any discussion concerning this particular issue, but be my guest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we conclude that in 1997, you didn't mention Stakic in this context at all?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, just as I mentioned Kovacevic and others. People were, psychologically speaking, under the impression that it was a Serb town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it, then, true that the officials of the Tribunal failed to reflect accurately what you stated?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did you find this, that this was not correctly stated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is a question the witness cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he had mentioned Stakic the first time as well. So either he didn't mention him, or the officials of the Tribunal failed to put his words in the statements. Your Honour, I'm trying to find out what is true, what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I don't think it changes anything. I mentioned that, but probably not everything was recorded. Now, I just mention that this was also the conviction of Srdjo Srdic, Stakic, Kovacevic, and others, many others, who attended the meetings on the division of power, that the Serbs had been betrayed. Now, whether I enumerated all of them in my statement, I didn't insist that all of them should be recorded because it was -- we were talking about Mr. Stakic specifically. But you cannot see from the text that there is no possibility that others said that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were signing your first statement which took place in 2001, did you point to this difference in the --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not really compare the two. It was not available to me, nor did I ask to do that. I know that I did not say things that I do not stand by, that I did not stand by or do not stand by. And I did not really see that there was a need for me to compare. I did not have the intention of really constructing a story. I know that -- I know that it cannot be that my statements would contradict one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, when did you hear Stakic say these things?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the last session of the Municipal Assembly held in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else with you listening to this?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cehajic, Kovacevic. It took place in the hall, also in front of the municipal building. But this took place in the conference room. It was said again that the Serbs were cheated out, and I did say that perhaps they were, to a certain extent, cheated out by the very system that existed before. None of them were satisfied, the Serbs, Bosniaks, or Croats. But as far as I know, they were not the -- the elections were not rigged. I know that a lot of in fact Bosniaks but Croats as well, Serbs, who voted for the SDA. But the Serbs simply could not accept what had happened, and I understand that they were angry. I can understand that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was it that you heard Dr. Kovacevic say these things?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did not take place only once. Ever since the elections, we were hearing that the Serbs were swindled, that there are more Serbs in Prijedor than other ethnicities, and this was the opinion held by the majority of the Serbs, because they were -- they could not accept the results of the census either. This was an issue, I think, of greatest -- that caused greatest misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your 1997 statement, page 3, paragraph 6; 739, paragraph 2 of the B/C/S version, you say, and I quote: "Kovacevic said that Prijedor would not join anyone but Serbia and that non-Serbs will never destroy Yugoslavia -- or break up Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that you held the same opinion. I would really like to hear how many Serbs actually did not hold such an opinion. 90 per cent of the Serbs advocated such a stance that they wanted Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you hear Dr. Kovacevic say these things?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On more than one occasion. Serbs really revolted at the division of Yugoslavia. This was a fact. I don't see that this can be a problem in the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall the specific occasion when you heard Dr. Kovacevic say these things?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the negotiations about the division of functions, I think that it took place during the discussions whether Basic would be appointed or Talundzic. And on several other occasions. Serbs in general said these things very often. This was something they criticised the Bosniaks mostly about, about the division of Yugoslavia, and this is a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your 2001 statement, page 4, paragraph 8 of the English version, or page 664, paragraph 3 of the B/C/S version, you said the same about Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I confirm what I said then, and I ask you: Was there a Serb who did not think this way?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is just merely a result of a presumption of yours?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was this said by Mr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stakic said this at the last meeting of the Municipal Assembly. I don't see any problem about that. It was him who said this about the division. This was when the last meeting was interrupted, and he had a right to be fond of Yugoslavia. Why not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say this as well to the ICTY officers when you were giving a statement about Mr. Kovacevic in 1997? Was it at that time that you also mentioned Mr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably I said that it was true for everyone, because this was -- this opinion of Serbs was very prominent at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then confirm that again the ICTY officers did not record your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say about what the ICTY officers did. I just said what the people at the time said during the negotiations for the division of functions, and I heard it myself from Stakic in the venue of the meeting of the Municipal Assembly. This was the theatre building, and this was a fact. And I think we can say that this was a fact, this was true that the Serbs thought they held Slovenians, Croats, and Bosniaks responsible for the breakup of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3, paragraph 6, line 3 of the English version, or page 739, paragraph 2, line 5 of the B/C/S version, you say: "Kovacevic said that non-Serbs do not -- had no right to ask for authority and that they had falsified the elections." On page 2, paragraph 5, line 3 of the English version of your statement dated 2001, or 602, paragraph 5, line 5 of the B/C/S version of the same statement, you said: "He" -- and you meant Stakic -- "also said that non-Serbs had no right to ask for authority and that the Serbs had always been cheated in peace."

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see that there is any contradiction here. I explained it a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mention this as well to the ICTY officers when you were giving your statement in 1997?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? What did I mention?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were giving a statement for the case of Dr. Kovacevic, did you at the time mention Dr. Stakic as well?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see what is at issue here, because then it was Dr. Kovacevic who was at the centre, and today it's Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even at that time, the ICTY officers did not record your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is your -- that is how you see it, and that is not how I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will rephrase my question, then. Did the ICTY officers record in the written statement everything that you said? Or did they actually select what to record and what not to record?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an issue that we can discuss. I think perhaps I should answer it this way: I think that they recorded what was relevant for a given subject, topic. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were being asked questions by the ICTY officers, did they ask you to speak only about Dr. Kovacevic, or did they ask you to speak about the events that took place in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, we were talking mostly about the events involving Dr. Kovacevic. Of course, in the process, we spoke of other issues as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3, paragraph 3, line 7 of the English version of the 1997 statement; the B/C/S version, page 739, paragraph 2, line 6, you said: "He" -- and you mean Kovacevic -- "also accused Dzevad Seric" --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzad Seric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have Dzevad Seric here.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, in the statement it says Dzevad, but thank you for your assistance. So you say: "He" -- meaning Kovacevic -- "also accused Nedzad Seric, the president of the Court in Prijedor, of falsifying the results of the elections." On page 2, paragraph 5, line 6 of the English version of your statement dated 2001, or page 662, paragraph 5, line 6 of the B/C/S version, you say: "He" -- and you mean Stakic -- "repeated several times that non-Serbs had falsified the elections, and he also accused the president of the court in Prijedor, Mr. Seric, of falsifying the results of the elections."

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone accused Seric, even Srdic. They all accused Seric as the one who was to blame most for the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you hear Mr. Kovacevic say this?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the negotiations about the division of the functions. And as for Mr. Stakic, I told you that I met him twice during the negotiations, and I didn't hear him say that during these discussions. But in the theatre, when we had this last meeting of the Municipal Assembly that was interrupted, it was then that I heard -- that he said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you certain that Mr. Stakic participated in the negotiations for the division of power?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did not take part to a great extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was a member of the delegation that negotiated the division of power?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mention to the ICTY officers -- did you mention to them Mr. Stakic in 1997?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was not the subject that we discussed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can actually conclude that you did not mention Mr. Stakic in 1997?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now ask you about an issue concerning mobilisation. Can you recall how many people were mobilised in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I know that there were young people who joined the military service, but I don't know the exact numbers. I know that many people decided not to respond to these calls amongst Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will have to rephrase my question, because it was entered in the records wrongly. Do you know how many times, on how many occasions, were mobilisation -- were people called up? On how many occasions before the war?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that there were several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there -- did it happen on one or two occasions that people were called up?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the one who was at all on the list to be called up, so I did not really -- I was not a conscript. I did not really know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, do Your Honours think that this would be the appropriate time to have the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. We adjourn until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated, and let's immediately proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we continue, Mr. Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask you again about the mobilisation, because this is where we left off. But if you don't know much about this subject, please let me know. Are you aware that the mobilisations were called up in September and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dates when they were called up. All I know was that at one point in time, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the SDA expressed its support to any of these mobilisations or to one of them?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not in favour, the mobilisation, in particular, those who were not willing to go to Croatia to fight war there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an interparty agreement in this respect?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in any such negotiations, and I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that those who wished to go were allowed to go, and those who did not wish to go did not have to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified that the Serb propaganda was, for the most part, targeted against the SDA?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only against the SDA, but against the HDZ and Bosniaks in general, because the Serbs felt that they had been cheated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3, last two lines of the English version of your statement given in 2001, that is, page 663, paragraph 4 of the B/C/S version, you declare that you heard Stakic speak on the Prijedor Radio and say that the Serbs had been cheated and that this could not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that this was unacceptable for Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember when it was that you heard this?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the last session. The last session of the municipality of Prijedor when they discussed the situation and their activities in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you heard this over the radio. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the session, like I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you remember --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the date?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just prior to the outbreak of the conflict in Prijedor, some ten days before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the session which was eventually interrupted and which you attended, too?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that those were the words of Mr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was announced. He took the floor, and he entered into an agreement with Mr. Cehajic. And it was Mr. Cehajic who kept repeating his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be able for you to recognise the tone of voice of Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that someone at the Prijedor Radio had Dr. Stakic's speech.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out whether you can recognise the voice of Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, and I think that I said that already, that Mr. Stakic said that, repeated that, even at the time when I was present. So I don't think that the quality of his voice is now very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the vice-president of the SDA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You advocated a peaceful solution to the disagreements?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I still do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you replaced in the party?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not replaced. There were internal elections within the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you obtain support of the party members?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should ask them. But you're probably interested in what I think of these internal elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, tell us what you think.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some people probably did not like my approach, my attitude. That's one possibility. But I don't know exactly what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that it was very difficult for Muslims to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was difficult for me as well. Some Bosniaks left Prijedor relatively easy; some with difficulty. I don't know what the reason for that was. I addressed myself on three occasions to various organisations with the purpose of leaving Prijedor. And soon after I submitted my request, some of these organisations stopped working. Again, why that happened at the time that I wanted to leave the town or someone else, I don't know. There were probably some minor difficulties, minor problems, regarding this, regarding departing Prijedor. But again, that's just my opinion. One of the reasons why it was difficult at the time to leave the town was the requirements to have transit visas for Croatia. Another problem was money, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was possible for military-age Serbs to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I very much doubt so. It was probably possible for some of them, but the number, I guess, would have been very small. If you are referring to the period of time following the conflict of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, that's the period of time I have in mind. Thank you. In 1997, were you ever a guest speaker at the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never addressed the assembly of the Prijedor municipality. I was just a guest in the sense that I was present to see how its work would unfold. And in a sense, I also influenced Bosniaks, persuading them that they should come to attend this session of the assembly, because there was a discussion involving the national anthem, the flag, the official flag and so on and so forth. And I insisted that the Serb decision should be respected. Of course, they have the perfect right to stand by their interests, but the others did not have to accept that. However, it was my opinion that they should be present and cooperate. So I didn't actually take the floor at the session. It was simply a conversation, a discussion, between the representatives of the coalition and the Serb side. I merely spoke to the representatives of the Bosniak side and the members of some of the parties, but this discussion was unofficial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible for you to attend the assembly sessions in a certain capacity?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I told you, at the time, I was a party member. This is the time that I indicated that my occupation was politician. I was a professional at the time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what particular function you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I represented the Party of Democratic Action of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I heard you, but however, once again, for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1997, I was the president of the SDA for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you testified on page 8, line 25, that the humanitarian aid reached Bosnia from Germany even before the war.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any need for humanitarian aid in Bosnia before the war?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I said "before the war," I was referring to the conflict in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So before the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because there were already problems with, for instance, baby food and some other supplies. Some of the roads had already been blocked. And as I indicated, 50 per cent of this humanitarian aid went to the organisation called Kolo Srpskih Sestara. 25 per cent went to the Caritas, and 25 per cent to Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These difficulties with the supplies of goods, did they influence the overall availability of goods and commodities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation in which local Prijedor companies found themselves at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the situation was. I mean, I don't know exactly what it was, but I'm sure that it was much worse than it had been before the conflict in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the president of Merhamet, were you aware of the existence of refugees, of the presence of refugees, in the territory of the Prijedor municipality? I'm referring to refugees from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Prijedor at the time. I just heard that the refugees from Krajina, that is, from Croatia, had arrived as a result of the combat operations in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that there were refugees from Croatia as early as in late 1991 and early 1992 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the number was not yet very high. I know that the International Red Cross distributed food and other types of assistance for this category of people as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about the refugees from the Bosanska Bojna that arrived in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, in your statement, on page 16, line 20, you said that a camp was established for Serbs who did not follow the official policy.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the location of this camp, do you know?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Prijedor -- this was a place where tyres were being repaired, of dampers, bulldozers used for the work in the mine. So this was the place where these tyres were being repaired. I heard this from a couple of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when this camp was established?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, but I think it was in existence in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until what time was it in operation?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably even after I had left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, on how many occasions did you find yourself in the company of Mr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on many. Perhaps two or three times during the negotiations, and the last time that I attended this session of the Municipal Assembly. If you mean amongst other people, that we discussed, that he was present there, yes. But of course, I -- just seeing him, I did see him on more occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You speak of this last session of the Municipal Assembly, and you say that you entered the theatre where the session was being held. Was there security around?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time, the session was already over, and many deputies were leaving. On this particular location, there is a cafe today. So it was there that people would move around, and the deputies in the assembly would actually meet there and discuss issues. So it was no really official premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 22 of yesterday's transcript, line 11, when asked by the Prosecutor whether you met with Mr. Stakic on some other occasions apart from this last session of the Municipal Assembly, as you said, then you said you never met him again.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 20 of yesterday's transcript, line 16, you stated that the Serbs kept saying that they were constantly outvoted.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they outvoted?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably in some issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Milomir Stakic in the company of Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this last session at the assembly, it was with him that he talked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On some other occasion perhaps?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Often, even when I wasn't part of the company, I would see them together on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On yesterday's transcript, page 14, line 14, when asked by the Prosecutor as to who represented the SDS in the negotiations for the division of power, you said that there were people from the military, Arsic and others.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these negotiations take place in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you want to say that Arsic was a member of SDS in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying this. I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't all the officers of the JNA have to be members of the alliance of communists at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the policy. They had to be members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, then, that it was impossible for a person to be an officer of the JNA and to be a member of a party other than the League of Communists of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since in former Yugoslavia, there were no other parties, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about 1991 when there were other parties.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But at that time, you didn't have the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had the League of Communists, the movement for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to clarify this. When there were discussions about the recruitment of young persons for the military service, then the discussions were held with Arsic and with the other one -- what was his name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, Zeljaja. And then it was said, of course, under the constitution, the persons had to go and serve the military service, and this is where the problem arose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did, then, the representatives of the military participate in the negotiations for the division of power?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, in this context, after division of power, no, because that day that I was referring to, we were discussing the military conscripts, because there were many people who tried to evade the drafting of the army, and that's when the military asked for an intervention of the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The announcements of the Crisis Staff broadcast on the radio, were they read by Stakic or by the announcer of the Prijedor Radio?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The announcer of the Prijedor Radio, that is, the lady announcer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senija, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In today's transcript, page 26, line 10 -- yesterday's, sorry, you said that Milomir Stakic read these announcements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, where is the quote?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Page 26, line 10, yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid this is not the context. I'm quoting now from the top of my head, I'm aware that the witness said that it was not Dr. Stakic, but a lady announce -- making this announcement. And here the question was, and you have to quote correctly: "Did you ever hear Dr. Stakic on the radio?" Then the witness said "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness said: "Yes, he was one of those who kept repeating these claims and announcements which we would hear over the Radio Prijedor on a daily basis."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think the next sentence should be read also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, be fair, and quote in the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "And the presenter was a Bosniak lady who had to read this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, this is what the witness said immediately before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the context, I understood that he said that Mr. Stakic read the announcements as well. That's what I wanted to clarify. But anyway, thank you, Your Honour, for your help. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kapetanovic, yesterday, you tried to explain to us what the main source of the conflict between the SDS, HDZ, and SDA was. In your opinion, the essential conflict, was it around the issue whether Bosnia and Herzegovina should be -- become an independent state, or was the issue at hand something else?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is a very broad one. It can -- things can be interpreted in different ways depending on the period you're referring to. We talk about the plebiscite where most of the people decided that Bosnia and Herzegovina should become a recognised state, and that this was the wish of the majority of the people. And I understand that perhaps Serbs did not feel good about it. But if I may persuade you, it was also very difficult for me, just as there had been Serbs left in Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Montenegro, so were there Croats and Bosniaks as well. But in my opinion, it would have been better to have solved it peacefully and to struggle for the interests of one's people within the borders, territorial borders that were historically determined rather than try and solve the issue by war. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you of the opinion that Bosnia and Herzegovina should secede from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just explained a moment ago what my opinion is. And if you follow the transcript which is in English, you will see that I have said that I was sorry. And I said that in my opinion, it would have been better to have solved the issue peacefully and to have struggled for the interests of one's people in a democratic way, and that the results of the vote should have been respected, and we could not really adapt the results to our own wishes. The important thing was to actually respect the decision of the majority. I agree with you that the majority doesn't always have to mean quality as well, but this is the best -- and this is the best solution. But as democrats, we have to abide by the decision of the majority and struggle for the interests and the needs of the minority. You have a next question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to 1992, was the notion of the constitutionality of people known in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the constitutional provisions?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did secession require all the three majority peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina to agree or accept the change of the status of the republic and the change of the borders of the republic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the results themselves point to the fact that there were Serbs who accepted this. I don't see that any minority, either that of the Serb, Bosniaks, or Croats, that they all participated in the plebiscite, just as previously had been the case with Slovenia and Croatia. I wouldn't really agree with the statement that the Serbs did not vote in favour. Obviously, the group that voted against found it very difficult, and obviously this is what actually caused such a reaction to take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you are familiar with the constitutional provisions relating to the change of the status of the republic. Do you know that apart from the requirement that the majority of each of the peoples to accept this, that also a two-thirds majority, a qualified majority, is required, which is 66.6 per cent, and that the referendum itself was actually taken part in by some 64 per cent, the turnout was 64 per cent?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any data concerning that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 26, line 23 of yesterday's transcript, you spoke of the incident at Hambarine, and you said that not a single Serb was killed, only one was seriously wounded but he was not in a critical condition.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I heard on the Prijedor Radio from this Serb himself who gave a statement in the hospital. The one who was more seriously injured was actually transferred to the Banja Luka hospital. There were even witnesses who were present in the hospital at the time and who later confirmed this to me. He even explained to us how the whole thing went in Hambarine. He said that they had a military vehicle, and that the Bosniaks told them to stop, and that the one who was more seriously injured stopped but then continued driving even faster than before. And this is how they opened fire, and this is how it all happened. I think that you will also have an opportunity of hearing the witness himself who worked in the hospital at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of a military vehicle was it?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A jeep. That's what I heard, what I was told. I did not see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were in that Jeep?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I was told, there were three of them. That is what this person who was injured was saying. Another version mentioned six. What is actually true, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know at least what happened to the third person?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he was wounded. The one who was only slightly wounded spoke for the Prijedor Radio. That is what he said. As to what actually happened, I don't know. I couldn't tell you because I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 27, line 14 of yesterday's transcript, you stated that there had been Serbs who had been killed in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated that some Serbs claimed in respect of them that they had been killed somewhere in the vicinity of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what the -- that was the story that went around in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it both from Serbs and Bosniaks. But I'm more inclined to believe the statement of the man who was in the vehicle and who was wounded. They went to the hospital to interview him, and he spoke into the microphone shortly after that. Shortly after the incident, he was broadcast over the Prijedor Radio. But soon after that, the story changed. There are several versions of the story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a name of any Serb who said this?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's a very good idea for me to mention such a name. I don't think that we have reached that degree of tolerance, that is, that we are able to accept other people's opinions. I think that the situation in Bosnia is still such that this is not possible. Of course, an end should be put to that. I do not wish the Serbs to feel that this Tribunal is working against them. I don't think that either Serbs or Croats should feel like that. I think that this Tribunal is working very well, and I can only express my gratitude to the Tribunal for that. But I know that people interpret things they hear in their own way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be prepared to give us the name of this individual if we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
