utterances.text: No. Not yet. Perhaps later, one day. But as I told you, there was a member of the staff who brought food to me. I was trying to tell you that there are Serbs and that there were Serbs who were not in favour of a war at any cost. But I hope that one day it will be possible for me to say loud and clear who that Serb was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there Serbian houses in Bosnia which were built in the traditional Bosniak manner? That is, with the windows facing all four sides of the house?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the existence of a Crisis Staff of the SDA which was established in Hambarine in the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about that, but I don't know exactly. I believe that it existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear who the members of the Crisis Staff were?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that it was Mirza Mujadzic, Hilmo Hopovac, Talundzic, and some others whose names now escape me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were yesterday asked questions by the Prosecutor concerning a press article which was shown to you. Did you ever see this article before?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what its origin is?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It comes from Kozarski Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you base your conclusion on what you were able to read on the photocopy?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe it to be true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of person Milomir Stakic is?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I declared something to that effect in my statement, and I also said that I agreed with the statement made by the journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly did you tell us what kind of person Milomir Stakic is?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say anything specific as to how he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it that you agreed with, with the journalist?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with everything that is contained at the beginning of the article, in the first statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know now what you agreed with?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you repeat this for us?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can. I think that this is a provocation. My memory doesn't always serve me right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to hear what you accepted to be the characteristics of Milomir Stakic and the traits of his personality.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what the journalist said, and if you have read the article, you will know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you accepted the opinion of the journalist without giving any comment?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, without any comment, and I still refuse to comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 42, line 3 of yesterday's transcript, you wanted Milomir Stakic to tell you where it was that Bosniaks and Croats attacked Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milomir Stakic cannot give you his answer, but let me ask you something concerning these statements of yours. Have you ever heard of massacres at Sijekovac and Kupres which occurred in the month of March 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I heard, yes. I do not justify any massacre, as I told you yesterday at the beginning of my testimony. I think that the life of every man is sacred. I cannot accept that the humankind should destruct themselves. I think that this is terrible, and I also expressed my hope that all those who did this will eventually be punished by the Creator. And I also said that it was possible -- it was not possible for any court to punish all perpetrators, all people who are guilty and responsible. How do you go about punishing a person who killed 30 other men? In my opinion, on this world, it is not possible to mete every punishment deserved, to mete out every punishment. I can talk about my opinions, my positions, what I did or what I didn't do. If someone did something evil, it doesn't, of course, give me the right to act alike. I can understand that people can have a hard time. I was having a hard time. But after all that, I said that I appeal to this Honourable Chamber not to sentence Mr. Stakic to prison for what I personally have been through. I think that you were able to see what my position was. And I have the same attitude towards everyone. I think that all those who did something wrong or said something wrong will eventually be punished. I don't think that the life would have any meaning if finally each one of us is not given either a compensation or a sentence. We are all going through a number of trials, but we are all different. And that is what constitutes the richness of the humankind. We should all strive to be better human beings. And I said that I did not want Mr. Stakic to end up in prison just because of what I felt and went through during that period of time. I cannot, however, say this on behalf of anyone else. Every victim will have the right to -- and has the right to justice. If not now, in this life, then in some other life. I think that we will all meet our judgement. This is how I view things, and I'm -- I've been very pleased with your questions generally speaking, apart from some minor comments that you made now and then. But I think that generally speaking, your questioning was correct and fair. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I personally have profound respect for your opinions and your approach to life in general. However, I'm sure you're aware of the need that we are here with the purpose of establishing the truth.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am. That is the reason why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can we move on from these lofty issues and focus on reality for a change.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means, but this is all reality, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you again a few questions concerning the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the people who -- were the people who participated in this attack crazy?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that if they were treated in any psychiatric clinic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know who was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who it was who had pushed them into all this?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the decision of the then rump government of Bosnia and Herzegovina on stopping the columns of the JNA personnel and the attacks on barracks?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really. But I know that when Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised by the United Nations, it was a big question whether the decision, that is, the results of the plebiscite, should be respected or not. I'm referring to the Serb plebiscite, or whether to respect the decision of the United Nations. I think that they were in a big dilemma. Well, you called it a "rump presidency," and you are discussing the validity of their decisions. I have to say that I do not feel competent to answer such questions and to give such comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only wanted to ask you whether you have heard of a decision on the attack of columns and equipment of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of such decision, but I know for fact that such movement was indeed obstructed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of an attack on the column of JNA personnel in Tuzla in the month of April?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there was such an attack, but I didn't hear anything specific about it. All I know was that there were some problems in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not familiar with the number of casualties, with the number of soldiers who were killed?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the attack which took place in Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are now telling me an attack that happened in Sarajevo, whereas I was in Prijedor at the time under house arrest, and the electricity was very often cut off. The shortages were very frequent. Electricity would come and go, so I wasn't able to follow these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that the United Nations recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's that got to do with me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you spoke about --

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell me that there was no such recognition?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By no means. I just want to know whether you know when the country was recognised.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It's not important right now. The important thing is that it was recognised. You know it just as well as I do. You could see it on TV when the Bosnian flag was hoisted in the United Nations. Well, if you wish -- if it is your intention to compare the events and put them in context, then maybe, yes, you are right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move on from this subject. On page 30 of yesterday's transcript, line 19, you stated that there had been an order for Bosniaks and Croats to put up white sheets on their houses.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say: "For a while, we had to keep them out -- keep them up."

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about 15 days, I think, or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 46, line 13 of yesterday's transcript, you say that everyone knew on whose side Fikret Abdic was?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People traded with him, eggs, poultry, and poultry products coming from that company were sold in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So which party did Fikret Abdic belong to in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To SDA, everyone knows that. However one should inquire about his positions, the positions that he had in 1991, those that he had in 1992, and those that he had in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, he was a member of the Party for Democratic Action, was he not?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, officially speaking. However, unofficially, he already embraced different positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Mr. Abdic today?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia. I can see what you are alluding to. I didn't say that he sided only with Serbs or Croats; he merely thought that what he was doing was correct. But whether this was really so, I think time will show.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will refer now to an event that might be traumatic for you. The fact that your children were beaten during one of the searches, was this traumatic for you? Was this a traumatic event for you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anyone would be able to calmly watch someone else beat their children. And if you say it's traumatic, I don't really know what you imply by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I meant was that this was a really unpleasant event.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unpleasant definitely. Traumatic can have can have other connotations. This is why I did not accept this definition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is something you will always remember?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you explain the fact that you never mentioned this incident earlier, but only yesterday here, before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered to you a moment ago that I do not intend to keep recalling and repeating this. I think this would be disastrous for a person to keep thinking about one's problems. My approach to problems is a positive one, even when I'm beaten, I always try to look at it positively. Maybe at how -- what I will turn out to be later on. I don't want to have a shred of hatred in me or in my children. The problems lies with the perpetrators. They have a problem. My problem is to try and be -- and improve myself and be better, and this is why I never mentioned this. I wouldn't even like my children, my grandchildren, to have a shred of hatred in them, because this is something that destroys the very person who hates, not the person who is hated. This is how I see this, and I act in accordance with my opinion, and I try to have my family live this way. And I would really like the majority of the people to share this opinion of mine, but of course everyone has their own right to live the way they like. This is democracy. You can go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your family with you in Prijedor until you left Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there people who left Prijedor prior to 30th April? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean prior to the conflict in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, people were leaving, and a few of them were leaving because they were afraid of bad things happening in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Please bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have no further questions, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Mr. Kapetanovic, thank you for your patience and your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We should not forget, you tendered two exhibits. I have before me only the English versions. Did you tender also the versions of the former statements in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: , yes, Your Honour, we would like to tender all the statements into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the usher please provide us with those documents in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are two statements, both in B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But we should like to see the documents also in B/C/S. Then, are there objections from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. It's a generic objection against admitting the statements. My concern is first that it would tend to violate the principal that the evidence should come in under oral testimony under oath of the witnesses. And secondly, my concern is just more practical, if we tender for all the witnesses their prior statements, it creates, I think, unnecessary amount of documents, paperwork, and translations into the third language, which would be French. I don't think that's necessary when the witness has testified and we have a French transcript. He has been confronted with inconsistencies in those statements and has responded and all of that is in the transcript of his oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I've got your point, but here, it seems to be a clear exception. And during the break, the Judges discussed this issue. Here, it's not, in principle, a question of the content, first of all, of both documents but the quality, the special quality. And therefore, the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I qualify my objection. I understand Your Honours' point, and I see very much the point of that regarding these two statements, but perhaps it would be of assistance to everyone I would suggest if the Court only takes the English version. The B/C/S version is just a translation of the English that's made available mainly for the accused's purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But it's also important to see where we can find signatures and where we can find no signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this is -- we can maybe perhaps enter into an agreement, this is the procedure of the OTP. I can tell the Court, and I think the Defence, both counsel having sat through trials is aware of this. The statements are taken in English, and it's read back by an interpreter who translates it in the field. It's only back in the OTP, in the CLSS, the translation section, that it's then translated into the language of the accused. So the witness, not just this one witness, but none of the witnesses sign the B/C/S. I think we can stipulate to that among the parties. The only version which would be signed is the English, which is taken in the field. Would the Defence agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would agree with that, only this witness recognised B/C/S version of his statement when given the statement to sign in 2001, his statement from 1997. So that's only why they think that -- although we don't find any discrepancies in between English and B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we should stick to that what I said before and what the Judges said during the break. It's necessary. When it probably comes to -- we have to come back to these documents, we should be aware which is what. And therefore, the witness statement of 2001 is admitted into evidence. Which number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be D4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Number D4A the English version, and D4B the B/C/S version. And then, the draft witness statement of 1997, signed 10th July 2001 will be Exhibit D4A, the English version, and D4B, the B/C/S version. Sorry, D5A, and D5B. Is there any request for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then probably we can make it short. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, Defence counsel touched upon the issue of these documents we just mentioned before. But to be -- to have a clear solution, we have before us, as it was said, the draft witness statement. In the original as of 1997, apparently there was no signature and no initials. But later on, we can find, and you authorised this with your testimony today, your signature of 10 July 2001. Was there any reason in 1997 why you did not sign the document in 1997?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When there was the next interview in 2001, was it in the beginning or in the end of your interview of 2001 that you were asked also to sign the former interview?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were discussing this statement as well, and then I said that I agree, that I accept everything that I had said previously, and then I signed it. I don't see that there are any contradictions between these two statements, the one taken in 1997 and the one taken in 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for your better understanding, I have to come back to your -- our transcript of today, page 22, line 2. There you said: "I did not really compare the two. It was not available to me, nor did I ask to do that." My question is, was this as it is called "draft witness statement" read by you or was it read out to you in a language you understand? Because it will apparently be difficult for you to remember what you have said four years before.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was read out to me, my statement made in 1997, and I said that it was fine. They asked me whether I wanted to sign it, and I said yes. And I didn't compare the two texts. There was an officer who came up to me and asked whether I agreed to sign this, so I didn't have these two documents one next to the other. I agreed with the text, of course, so I -- but I didn't get a copy for me to be able to compare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In which language was this document of 1997 read out to you?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnian. There was an interpreter who interpreted for me the text in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think, then, we have clarification enough on this issue. One final question from my side: Yesterday, in your statement on page 45, line 23, following until page 46, line 3, you said: "I don't have an example, nor did I hear from anyone that Mr. Stakic killed someone or did something really bad to anyone. However, my major criticism of Mr. Stakic is that he failed to put some additional effort and to do something. I think that Serbs, having conducted themselves in this manner, lost more than they gained as we lost, Croats, and Muslims, and Serbs alike." For the better understanding of the Judges, could you be a little bit more concrete. What is your major criticism of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said this, I meant that -- well, I know that I, myself, did my best to improve the situation as far as I could, being a president of Merhamet. I put as much effort as I could to prevent the things that happened. And I said that I never heard from any Bosniak that Stakic personally killed anyone, and this is why I cannot accuse him of having done that. But I did say that if he could, he should have done more to prevent what happened because he held a responsible position. This is how I see it. I do not know if he was under pressure from someone else that prevented him from doing more. This was the issue, this was what I said. This is the question -- this is the question that I put also here today, perhaps in a different manner, but the meaning is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these additional remarks. Judge Fassi Fihri, please. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] When you heard announcements of Dr. Stakic over the radio, did you actually hear his name? Was his name pronounced?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever a deputy in the assembly was there to talk, then he was announced, and then he commented on it. And of course, whoever held the microphone commented on it. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Because you told us that such announcements, such declarations, were made almost on a daily basis. Were all these declarations attributed to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the judge, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the announcement that he made, this is what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, when have you heard about Dr. Stakic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the negotiations between the SDA and the SDS were taking place in the Prijedor municipality building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the role and action of Dr. Stakic in the events before the takeover and after the April 1992 takeover in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in his private life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But I mean not his private life, but his public life, as politician.

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that he represented the SDS party when he was still the president of the SDS -- vice-president of the SDS. When Srdjo Srdic was president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And how often did Dr. Stakic make public statements on TV, radio, and newspapers, or public meetings, before and after the takeover in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he gave statements very rarely. He did, but rarely. As far as I can tell, I cannot recall many of his statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Well, in your statement made on the 17th of July in year 2001, you said that "Stakic was repeating in interviews, public appearances," and it's page 4 of the English version. "Stakic was repeating in interviews, public appearances, and in local community meetings that the Serbdom, was in jeopardy, that Serbs had to stay together in one state." What is the meaning of "Serbdom"? In your opinion, what did Dr. Stakic mean when referring to "Serbdom"?

utterances.speaker: NIJAZ KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have to distinguish between these interviews and his statements made at different meetings, in local communities. What does "Serbdom" mean, perhaps the question should be addressed to Mr. Stakic. I didn't know what he meant by "Serbs" and "Serbdom." I said that this was detrimental to Serbs, Croats, and Muslims alike. What it meant precisely to him, that, I cannot say. I can perhaps look at it as a body of spiritual, cultural, traditional values of a people that need to be respected. What he meant by that is something I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Hereby we conclude your testimony, and we thank you very much for the informations and your very human approach you let us know. And you are excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We stay adjourned until 12.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Dr. Cehajic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic, you can understand me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So first of all, welcome. And our apologies for the delay. But we should start immediately. And would the usher please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The examination may start, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For the record, Ann Sutherland from the Office of the Prosecutor has joined us after the break, and she will conduct the examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Excuse me, usher, would you be able to move the ELMO thing down because it's in the road of the witness. The machine, the ELMO machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Take the entire machine away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: My name is Minka Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 20th of March, 1939, in Ljubija, in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your nationality or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you practice a religion?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I practice religion in my own way. I think that all people are religious in their own way. I was born in a family that practiced religion, but not very strictly. But I can say that I was raised in a religious spirit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that religion Islam?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1968, you completed your medical degree. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1968 until 1992, you lived and worked in the city of Prijedor in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First as a medical doctor in the Mladen Stojanovic medical centre?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a general practitioner before I completed my specialist training and consequently became a pediatrician. But this was all within the same medical institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also specialised in nephrology, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: That is the so-called subspecialisation which I completed in 1983 and 1984 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1977, did you occupy the head of the children's section in the Prijedor hospital?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was after I passed my specialist examination. In the month of June, I became as a result of that, the chief of pediatrics, and worked there up until maybe two years before the war -- four years before the war when I became deputy chief of the hospital, deputy manager of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from February 1993 until February 1994, you worked in Croatia as a physician for mothers and children at the Doctors of the World clinic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked as a physician at the children's health centre, mother and children's centre, which was financed by humanitarian organisation in France, Les Medecins du Monde, and this is where I work as a pediatrician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since 1996, you have been working in a clinic as a pediatrician?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll repeat it. Since 1996, you have been working in a clinic as a pediatrician?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: 1996 -- no. I have been working from 1996 in Sanski Most in a clinic -- well, it's actually hospital but you use the word clinic. But the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, were you married?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe my status. My husband is missing. I am married.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year did you get married?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I married Muhamed Cehajic. He was already working as a professor at the time while I was still a student.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have two children, a daughter age 37, and a son age 30?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that your husband was a professor. What was he a professor of?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: He taught what was at that time called Serbo-Croatian language and philosophy, and he has a degree in world literature and philosophy from the Sarajevo university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had he been teaching for up until 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: He had been teaching in Prijedor ever since 1966 until 1991, 1992, when he switched to another function. Until that time, he had worked at the local grammar school in Prijedor. But before that, he also had another teaching post in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If we correctly heard the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he also had another teaching post in Banja Luka. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: No. No. Maybe it was misinterpreted. He never taught in Banja Luka. I was in Banja Luka for a period of time to undergo a training, so he came to visit me, but he taught in Sanski Most before he taught in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you lived in Banja Luka in 1968. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: No. We lived in Ljubija. We didn't have an apartment in Prijedor, so he, at the time, was living with my mother, and I was living temporarily in Banja Luka, because I was participating in a compulsory medical course. So from time to time, he would visit me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: At what time? During what period of time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband join a political party in the late 1980s?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes -- no. Not in late 1980s. It was in 1991 that he became a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband hold an executive position within the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't have an executive function within the SDA. He was a member thereof. And as such, he was at one point in time elected mayor as a representative of this party. As for any specific executive function before that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he elected mayor as a result of the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was mayor of the Municipal Assembly of the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of your profession, and also as a result of living in Prijedor for so many years, did you know many people from the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: As a result of my profession, I did know many people there. Some I knew by name; some I knew just by my sight because that was the nature of my profession. I had numerous contacts with various kinds of people. And almost every citizen of Prijedor at one point in time, he or his family member came into contact with me as a physician. So as a result of my profession, I knew more people in Prijedor than my husband did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your husband was elected mayor of the municipality. As a result of the 1990 elections, who was elected as your husband's deputy?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Milomir Stakic was elected as his deputy. There were two more functions, leading functions, within the municipality, that of the president of the Executive Board and his deputy. This information was published in Kozarski Vjesnik together with their four pictures. The photographs were taken as they were giving the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just pause there for a moment, we will discuss the president of the Executive Board in a moment. Just going back to Dr. Milomir Stakic, do you recall what political party he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: SDA and SDS divided the functions between themselves, because neither of them received more than 50 per cent of the votes. So it was necessary for -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment. My question was did you know what political party Dr. Milomir Stakic belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. He belonged to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what his ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe I did. He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Stakic prior to this appointment?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I may have heard of him. I knew most of the Prijedor doctors by name, but I had not personally seen him until that time. I may have met him in passing, but I didn't personally know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw a photograph in the newspaper. Do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can recall the date. But I remember that there was a comment made at work. When I came to work that day at the hospital, I saw this issue of Kozarski Vjesnik and these photographs. A colleague of mine commented on how they were dressed. This colleague was a Serb. And then he said to this other person: "Why didn't you put on suits? Why did you wear just pullovers?" Actually two of them were wearing pullovers and two of them were wearing suits. My husband and another gentleman were wearing suits, and these two other persons were wearing pullovers. That was the comment that was made at the time, and that is probably the reason why I remember this particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first see Dr. Stakic in person?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: After this photograph was published, I probably saw him a couple of times around the town. I never had any official meetings with him, so I don't remember when I first saw him. When I came to see my husband at work, I realised that they had they had their offices next to one another, only a corridor separated their two offices. The entrance of the building was common to both of them, and I remember seeing him there when I went to visit my husband in his office. That is one occasion that I remember. I don't specifically recall any other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly. Do you know who was elected to that position?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. It was a colleague of mine who worked with me at the hospital. I met him on a daily basis. That was Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what political party he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: He, too, was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he was a colleague of yours. How many years had you known Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I had known him ever since he came to Prijedor to work there sometime in the 1980s, 1984 or 1985. It must have been in the first half of the 1980s. Prior to that, he had worked somewhere in Germany, and he came to work to our hospital. We didn't have an anaesthesiologist at the time, so he came to fill the post. And it is since that period of time that I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you surprised at Kovacevic's appointment?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Not really. No. No, I wasn't. It was the time when the multiparty system was beginning to be implemented. There were several different political parties at the time already. So it was -- it didn't come as a surprise actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Prijedor when the Serbs took control on the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened that morning?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: That morning, I think I slept in a little bit. The telephone rang, and I answered the phone. It was Sadeta Medunjanin, a teacher who knew my husband. I didn't know her very well although she comes originally from Prijedor. I just knew her by sight. She was the one who called. And she said: "Did you hear what happened?" And said I didn't. She didn't go into details over the telephone. She just said: "Well, turn on the radio. You will hear." Which is what I did and heard this announcement broadcast over the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I -- at this point I cannot recall the contents in detail, but the sense of the announcement was that the Serbs had taken over power in Prijedor. This is what I remember, and that everything had gone smoothly without a single bullet having been fired, and that the Serbs had taken over. I'm just paraphrasing now the contents of the announcement, but that was more or less the idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I looked through the window, and I saw two soldiers outside the entrance to my building. It was time for me to go to work. I didn't know how to go to work. I called the hospital where I worked, and the driver who used to drive me when it was necessary -- of course, I went to work in my own car. But this time, I called him just to see first of all whether he was already there, and then I called him and I went to work in this official vehicle. Nobody created any problems because of that. But on the way to work, I could see that something was going on, that there were many people around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you reached the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Once I got to the hospital, I saw that the SDS flag had been put up outside the hospital and that there were soldiers and guards standing outside the entrance. However, I got in without any major problems or difficulties. I went about doing my regular job. It was on 30th of April, and the 1st May was an official holiday. So it was customary for me to check that everything was all right at various departments, that people were there, that personnel was at work, that the equipment was as it should be. So I went about checking all this, and I didn't realise that anything really tragic was going on on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, if I could just ask you to slow down a little bit for the interpreters. You mentioned that about four and a half years before the war, you became deputy director of the hospital. Who was the director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: It was Dr. Tesinic, Nikola Tesinic, an eye doctor who was head of hospital at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnicity Dr. Tesinic was?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said when you got to work that day, you carried on as normal. Did you and Dr. Tesinic have to issue any paperwork to any staff member?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: There was staff members who expressed a desire to leave earlier. I don't know whether he had received any special instructions or anything, but we signed papers to that effect. That is, for all those who wished to leave before 3.00 p.m., which was the official end of the working day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did staff have to have a pass to enter the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: No. At the time I worked there, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that change from after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what change you have in mind. As I said, that day passed normally without problems. I performed my duties in the usual manner, as I had done before. Later --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, continue.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that the situation changed later in the following days. On that day, nothing unusual happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the situation change after that day?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I was already feeling uncomfortable because the atmosphere changed amongst the people. I heard that many managers were dismissed in Prijedor, that others had already been appointed to their positions. And in terms of employment, the situation was slowly becoming insecure. But I continued coming to work. Nothing happened as far as I was concerned. Nobody told me anything. So that period of time, until I finally left, I was fine. Maybe thanks to the colleague who trusted me. But he made me feel more or less safe despite the overall situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Doctor, excuse me, if we can just go back to the day of the takeover, what, if anything, did you hear on the radio later that day about the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: The radio broadcast kept repeating those announcements. But since I spent my time at work and then at home working, I didn't really pay much attention to it but I know that the same announcement was repeated on the radio several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything said on the radio about who would make decisions for the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or your husband speak with anyone from the Serb authorities in the days that followed the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I did not, but my husband did have phone conversations during the time that I was away at work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband instructed to do anything?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: In which period was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediately following the takeover.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I do not know of any special instructions. I know that there was a courier who brought a letter to him, a document, informing him that his functions have ceased, that he is on vacation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will discuss that in a moment. Was your husband asked to speak on radio?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, once. But I cannot remember the date. I did not hear his speech because I was at work, because every day I went to work. This is how things were happening after the -- until the 30th of May. But he did speak on the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who asked him to speak on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that your husband received a letter informing him that his functions had ceased, that he was on vacation. Do you recall when he received this letter?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same day, as soon as I came home, he told me: "I received this document by a person, a person who's a dispatcher in the assembly -- in the municipality" and who actually brought him the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the document signed by?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see the document. Probably it was signed by a person who replaced him. I didn't see the document. Even later, I did not recall to look at it. I only know he received it -- I cannot really confirm as to who signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who replaced your husband?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: My husband was replaced by Stakic, Milomir. So he was previously his deputy who became -- who assumed his position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of others who received the same letter that your husband did?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of this letter?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I do not. After a while, after he was taken away from home, they came to my house, and they took away anything of his personal documents that he had, including his identity card, his passport. So I had nothing left in written of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you continued to work.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was your last day of work?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband taken from your home to the police station for questioning?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well. It was the 23rd of May. It was afternoon, around 3.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he taken to the police station?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: There were persons in police uniforms who came and who said that he was supposed to be taken for an informative interview, and this is how they told me that he would perhaps return the same day but maybe during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he return that night?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: No. At 9.00 in the evening, a phone rang, and it was him personally speaking to me and telling me not to wait up for him, that he certainly wasn't going to come back that night but maybe tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend at the police station to find out about your husband?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, 24th of May, I went to the police, and I inquired after him. I asked if I could see him, and at the entrance, they told me that I could not see him. Then in this case, since I wasn't allowed to see him, I didn't have anything else to do but to go back home. And on my way home, I was walking on one side of the street, and I saw on the other side of the street Mico, Milan Kovacevic. He saw me, he greeted me. I approached him and told him that my husband been taken the night before. And I had been to the police station inquiring after him, and that I wasn't allowed to see him. And he told me: "Okay, you go back to the police station, and I will go to the municipality building, because the police building and the municipality building are just across one from another. He told me: "I will phone from there to the police station so that they allow you to see your husband." And so I returned to the police station. I sat there for a while in the waiting room --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just pause there for a moment, did Dr. Kovacevic seem surprised when you told him that your husband had been taken to the police station?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: He was not surprised. Well, I cannot say that he was surprised in any way, positively or negatively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned to the police station, were you allowed to see your husband?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they allowed me to see him, and that's when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything about your husband's condition when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: He seemed tired. I saw that his feet were swollen. I know that he had some problems with his heart, so I really paid attention to that. But he didn't tell me much about what had been going on. He just started talking about the people who were there with him, who were kept with him in the prison. And I told him that I wasn't interested about these people, but actually I was worried about us being eavesdropped by someone, so he stopped talking about other people. I interrupted him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit him again at the police station?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The next day, again, I visited him. They brought him without any intervention. I saw him again the same way, in the same room. But he already then was in a much worse shape. I brought him his glasses because I thought perhaps he will need his glasses. He was a person always reading books. But he told me: "I don't need my glasses. Take them back home. It's all over with me." Something in this sense. And then I told him: "Well, don't take it so badly. You are in prison because you have a political -- different political opinion. It doesn't mean that you are to blame for anything. Things will turn out fine." This is how we talked. I tried to raise his courage a bit. And that was the last time that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that he told you the names of some other people that had been detained with him. Do you recall the names of these people?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Just a bit. I have to adjust this. I can't hear it well. Now I can hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that he told you the names of the other people that were detained with him. Do you recall the names of these people?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember Zeljko Sikora. He was a physician working at the hospital. He was a younger person. He was -- he used to be a student of my husband's. He also told me about Ilijaz Music, and perhaps also Muharem Murselovic. But I interrupted him. Perhaps he would have told me some other names, but then he stopped. But he managed to tell me about these two persons, because he didn't realise that perhaps he wasn't supposed to tell me this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their ethnicities and what were their professions, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I know the teacher was Bosniak, and Dr. Sikora, Zeljko was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "the teacher." What's the surname of the teacher?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: He was a professor, not a teacher. Music, Ilijaz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that was the last day that you saw your husband. Did you try and visit him again?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The following day, I thought that he was still at the police station, but I couldn't go out because I was on duty. I was working for eight hours, but then I prolonged my duty until the 27th May, the morning of the 27th. So I asked my colleague to write a pass for me to be able to go out, because I told him I wanted to go and see what was happening with my husband. So when I arrived at the police station, I was told that he was already away and that he was -- that he had been transferred to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I wasn't allowed to go to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: There was -- the military there was present in large numbers, and I knew that I would have problems if anyone intercepted me. I knew that I would have to have a pass to move around the town, and I didn't want to obtain a pass. So I knew that I wasn't supposed to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who issued these passes to move about the town?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I never tried to obtain one, but I was told that it was in the Crisis Staff that one would get them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you continued working until the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened at work that day.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, I ended my duty. I actually was frightened to stay in the hospital because the hospital was full of soldiers. I don't know what they were doing there, but there was a lot of them, and I had this pressing need to go and see my husband. So I asked a colleague of mine to write for me a document allowing me to go on vacation, and also some days off, because I had some days off after my duty. I wanted to stay at home and to relax a bit. My colleague told me: "Don't do this. I don't think it would be a very good idea for you to stop working. You'd better come to work. Things will be fine." He was laughing. He told me: "The only thing that they will do is they will remove the two of us. Somebody else will be running the hospital." I told him: "Well, I didn't really care about that." So I did go home. I decided that I would not go on vacation. But in the evening, someone --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause there. Whilst you were at work, the colleague you referred to earlier, was that your superior, Dr. Tesinic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was the only one that I actually communicated with in that period. It was him that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry I interrupted you. You were about to say: "In the evening."

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Someone informed my brother that I was not supposed to show up in the hospital the next morning, and I did not. And the following day, a nurse who was a neighbour of mine brought me a document saying that as of yesterday, I was on vacation. And then subsequently, I found out that that same morning, all the people who showed up for work were stopped by soldiers at the entrance. Those who were Serbs were allowed in. But also some Muslims who were obviously needed. But in general, Bosniaks and Croats were sent to go home. I didn't personally see it, because I was spared that since I had my vacation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Tesinic continue to work?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Not as a director, but as a physician, as an eye doctor on his -- in his department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who replaced Dr. Tesinic?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I know because I was told when I needed something, a favour, they told me that Dr. Radojka was now the director. I needed a favour from her, and this is why I phoned her by phone from home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was her last name?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Radojka Elenkov.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity was she?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You may have said it before. What was Dr. Tesinic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb. I said that already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he was replaced?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I do not know, but judging from what he told me, and the way he laughed about it, he probably was not a trusted person, since he was placed in the same category as myself to be removed from the position. Obviously, he was not as the person that was required for that position at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time. I'm just about to show the witness a document, so perhaps I can do that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can proceed with the document, first the document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown the document that's marked P650 in the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The ERN number for the B/C/S is P0055291, and the ERN number for the English translation is 03044478.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, what is the date of that document?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who has the document been issued by?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: By the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Province of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just read the text below the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Below?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where it says over to the right-hand side of the page.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: "Crisis Staff, Autonomous Region of Krajina".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it has the reference number and the date. Then the text on the right-hand side of the page under the date.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: "Copy, extracts from the conclusions of the Krajina, Autonomous Region, Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the date of the session of the autonomous region Krajina Crisis Staff in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: "At the session of the Crisis Staff of the Krajina Autonomous Region held on 3 May 1992, adopted the following..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that 3 May or 13 May?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: There is a 1 in front of 3. It's 1 and 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Crisis Staff conclusion, who was it sent to? Under the text on the right-hand side, does it say who it's sent to?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: "To all socially and privately owned enterprises."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read out the third paragraph under the "conclusion."

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: "In the managing positions of the enterprises in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina must be filled with people who are absolutely loyal".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose is the signature block just below that?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: President Radislav Brdjanin, and the authenticity of the translation is certified by -- well, Radislav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says: "The authenticity of this copy is certified by..." Can you read the name below that text.

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the text under the name?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's secretary of the secretariat for the economy, perhaps Travar. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the stamp that's on that document?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: "Prijedor, Municipal Assembly of Prijedor." "Prijedor Municipal Assembly," yes. "Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Ranko Travar?

utterances.speaker: MINKA CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that document can be returned to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we then conclude for the day, but before the document tendered. Objections by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. We do have objections to the document. Essentially the same as the prior on the document, and I recognise the Court's ruling that you will accept it, but this witness specifically stated that she didn't recognise the person. Hasn't laid the proper foundation thus far at least with her testimony to allow this document to come in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will be calling an investigator which will -- who will be able to give evidence as to the source of this document, where this document was seized from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As we said earlier, it's only the question whether or not this document exists. It may be a photocopy of an existing or not existing document. This is a question of evaluation of the evidence, and therefore this document is admitted into evidence as S48A in the English version, and S48B in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will also submit this document for a revised translation because in the English translation it does say "at its session of 3 May, 1992" when in fact on the B/C/S document, you can -- it can be seen it is 13th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can be sure we are aware of this problem. But we have to conclude for today. The trial stays adjourned until Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
